conflicts.outcome: The real-constraint override covers accessibility and no-JavaScript use, and reaches only as far as that duty: every page follows Design Release 2.1 except where it falls short of it. The 9 October afternoon ruling, which outranks every other source, makes every page work fully without JavaScript and replaces this conflict's earlier origin, transit, transporter and CPH clauses. Start and origin: keep the 'Error: ' title prefix on the type question and the origin page, a real 'Country of origin' label on an accessible-autocomplete over a native select that works without JavaScript, and the region code input linked to its hint and error with the error style; within that build the hint and placeholder follow Design Release 2.1, while opening on focus, matching, the arrow and the announcements follow the component as the real frontend configures it (c-009). Port of entry and transit countries: keep today's native selects, the Add country button and the Remove buttons that submit the form, and today's announcements; adding a country the moment it is picked, removing one without a page load and the custom announcement wording are settled by the 13 November design ruling; keep the 'Error: ' title prefix and the visually hidden country name on each Remove. Transporters: the list's in-page filter is blocked with transporter management, and the commercial form's fields hidden behind the address search wait on the address lookup; without JavaScript the commercial form shows its fields from the start. Upload documents: keep the 'Error: ' title prefix, the error summary at the top of the main content, the attachment error after its hint, Remove buttons naming their document and link text saying it opens in a new tab; everything else follows Design Release 2.1. CPH number: the page works as today with the server's checks, and the interaction designer's 9 November ruling settles that no type behaviour is added on top. Viewed notification: the title is '<reference> - Import notification service - GOV.UK' in every state, and the journey review keeps 'Review your notification - Import notification service - GOV.UK'. Success banners (the notification list's, the deletion message and the templates pages'): no auto-dismiss; a banner stays until the trader leaves or reloads the page, and everything else about it follows Design Release 2.1. The 26 November prototype adds two shortfalls the same duty covers: the type page's title gains no 'Error: ' prefix either, and without JavaScript the prototype's country search submits nothing; both are set aside. trace-prototype-dr2-1-p1-034 is not overruled although it records the box having no label: it still backs the 'Search for a country' placeholder and the decorative search button.

Cross-service and persistence constraints override the prototype's routing, where every type continues to the live-animals origin page and a plants draft takes a GBN-AG reference: Live animals continues to the animals frontend's live-animals start, which creates the GBN-AG draft and lands on origin, and origin's Back link returns to the type question. Paul's ruling of 5 November, which outranks it on this point, settles the vocabulary and the shape: the record and its API carry roles alone, 'use' is renamed 'role' everywhere, at least one role is required, no address type is stored, and the address type is the front door's grouping of roles (req-1256). The prototype's 'primary type' and 'category' fields are not copied, so prototype-dr2-1-source-p16-079 is kept only for what it says is stored, every ticked use. The address book on main already stores roles and no type (repo-addressbook-p1-002, p1-052) and the ticked roles reach the record (repo-tests-p13-036); the earlier untyped and unroled record no longer describes the service, so nothing here needs overruling. conflicts.about: Which countries the Country select offers: the prototype's fixed 42-country list, the frontend's own United Kingdom entry, or the reference data list.

inc-081: the real country list holds only sovereign states where DR1 offers regions and territories; blocked on MDM.

Countries come from the reference data service's countries endpoint.
The frontend drops any GB entry reference data returns and adds its own 'United Kingdom' entry.
In stub mode the captured countries fixture is used instead of a request.

conflicts.about: Where the address search's addresses come from: the prototype's made-up lists, or a real address lookup.

positions.says: inc-042 is kept for real addresses (c-178), but is blocked until the address lookup becomes a real feature.

The search keeps Design Release 2.1's look, but its results come from the INS backend's address lookup (req-1218), and all of it is blocked until the lookup becomes a real feature (c-217). A picked result fills the address fields; the lookup returns no organisation name, so the name is left for the user, and the country is United Kingdom because the search types are UK-only (req-1217). What else the search needs is settled when the area is re-distilled after the lookup lands.

conflicts.about: Whether add and edit keep length limits and an email format check that Design Release 2.1 does not have.

The edit form sets no format rule or message for email, phone or postcode, and no maximum lengths.
Email must be a well-formed email address, refused with 'Enter an email address in the correct format'.
Name may be at most 255 characters.

conflicts.outcome: The ruling's validation clause wins, and the germinal data fields' Standard Address Block, which outranks the prototype, sets exactly today's limits and an email-format email: today's length limits and email format check stay in the frontend and the API (req-1244). Postcode stays free text, as in every source; whether phone gains a format check is c-256.

conflicts.about: Whether an address book page's browser title keeps the 'Error: ' prefix when it shows errors, which the prototype leaves out.

The 26 November prototype has no search-only layout, so the earlier half of this conflict, error links to hidden fields, has nothing left to build (req-1285).

conflicts.about: Prototype persistence behaviour: addresses held only in the session, and an edited seeded address still listed with its old details.

After saving, the list shows the edited values under the same address.
After a rename the search shows one result whose View link points at the same address id as before.

conflicts.outcome: The ruling's persistence clause wins: addresses persist in the address-book service (req-1263), an edit saves its roles as req-1275 sets out, and the list shows what was saved (req-1276).

conflicts.about: Where templates live: the prototype's session with fifteen seeded templates, or real persistence.

positions.says: A real constraint the prototype cannot express, persistence among them, overrides the prototype.
This conflict is kept for a real constraint.
Templates, and deletions of seeded templates, are held only in the user's session.
Fifteen seeded templates follow the saved ones in the list.
dashboard-templates.js seeds seven templates dated 15 April 2026.

The live-animal seeds share internal reference N/A, Internal market and CPH 00/000/0000.
dashboard-templates-testing3.js seeds five live-animal templates dated 18 November 2026.
dashboard-templates-germinal.js seeds three germinal templates dated 20 November 2026.
Deleting a saved template that shares an id with a seed brings the seed back.
A template with no date created shows '15 April 2026'.
The prototype seeds 15 saved templates, 10 live animals and 5 germinal products.
The saved templates listed include five named seeds.

The list order (newest saved first), the count, the card and every page design still stand; only the session storage and the seed data are set aside, together with every other seed fixture claim, which req-1388 records. The prototype's clearing of its one in-session journey when a template is created or used is session storage too: real drafts are persisted, so creating or using a template leaves the user's other drafts untouched. Test suites may create their own templates through the journey.

conflicts.about: Who a stored template belongs to: the user who saved it, or their whole organisation.

Who can see a template, one user or the whole organisation, is not shown.
Persistence and authentication are real constraints that override the prototype.

conflicts.outcome: A saved template is private to the signed-in user who saved it and listed under 'My templates'; nobody else sees, uses, changes or deletes it. The prototype wins by default and keeps saved templates to the user who made them, held in their own session and listed under a 'My templates' heading; real persistence and sign-in, which the 7 October ruling ranks above the prototype, only replace the session with a store scoped to that user, whose shape is the backend's design. The prototype's shared seeds with no owner are set aside with the seeds themselves (c-183). The trace's gap claim is not overruled: it still records what the traces do not show.

The rendered page has the 'Sort by:' select with its four options.

The prototype's inert select and its options are set aside.

conflicts.about: Whether using a template copies the place of origin into every consignment party, as the prototype does for templates with no per-party addresses.

Cross-service behaviour and persistence override the prototype.

The copy of one place of origin into every party exists only for the seeded templates, which hold no per-party addresses, and is set aside: the real notification persists and sends each party separately, a cross-service constraint the prototype cannot express, and no seeded template is built (c-183).

A template saves the transporter's name, address, country, approval number and type.

A GET to /templates/save saves the template in progress with no confirmation.

Opening /templates/save during a template journey saves the template.

conflicts.about: Whether amend, cancel amendment and copy as new are started by links (GET) as the prototype draws them, or by form posts.

The action is a POST with crumb.

The prototype's claims are kept for where each control leads.

conflicts.about: Amend and cancel-amendment confirmations: a custom modal dialog (Design Release 2.1's cancel amendment) or a separate confirmation page (today's cancel-amend, the design's own amend page, the 9 October afternoon ruling, the interaction designer's answer).

positions.says: Cancel amendment is confirmed in a modal opened from the status line and the review page.
The cancel-amend modal is custom JavaScript and does nothing without it.
The cancel-amendment confirmation is a page at /notifications/{id}/cancel-amend.
None of plants' ending pages is a pop-up or dialog.
The prototype wins on look and feel unless a real constraint overrides it.
The amend and cancel confirmations stay separate pages and pop-ups are not built.
The dialog version waits on design in its own theme.
JavaScript-only prototype behaviour, pop-ups included, waits on design.
Amend and cancel amendment are pages, not dialogs.
Amend and cancel amendment are their own pages in the designs.
The waiting-on-design question on the dialogs is answered.

Amend lands on the Overview hub showing Amending.

positions.says: Confirming the delete removes the notification.
A deleted notification is only soft deleted: the record is marked deleted.

conflicts.about: Dashboard card actions: Copy as new and View only (DR1's card) or the status-driven set (today).

conflicts.about: Whether DR1's inc-026 (treat the delete and cancel-amend pages as unassessed, raise nothing about their copy) stops the Design Release 2.1 copy changes.

conflicts.about: What a copy carries over: Design Release 2.1's list, the backend copy's list, or everything but documents (what today's pages show).

positions.says: Copy as new uses the submitted notification's saved snapshot.
Copying an AMEND notification copies its current, in-progress answers.

conflicts.about: Where the guards, the delete and the view page's Back link send the trader: Design Release 2.1's overall dashboard, the INS front door, or the set's own notification list.

positions.says: The guard redirects land on the overall dashboard.

Every page the prototype sends to the overall dashboard goes to the set's own list.

The overall dashboard destination is the set's own list in every set.

That covers the delete landing, the refused amend, copy and cancel-amendment guards, the delete guard and the view page's Back link. DR1's note that the dashboard moves to the INS front door is not overruled here, because other areas still cite it for the INS home; the templates ruling supersedes its list move for this programme. Design Release 2.1's silent hold, which its own test calls a seed-format quirk, is overruled.

The rule that 'Save and continue' always offers the next page in journey order whatever the page was opened from (repo-frontend-p1-064) is set aside for pages opened from the overview, but the claim is not overruled because it still describes the opening run. Every chained-to page has its own overview row, so nothing becomes unreachable.

positions.says: Review notification is always a step after the contact address, and the next page after a step is the following step.
The review section opens only once the journey is ready for check your answers.

The consignment addresses page is the run's last step and already goes on to check your answers (repo-tests-p1-189), and the declaration still needs a complete notification. The review section's own readiness gate (repo-frontend-p1-053) is not set aside as a claim, because it also records the three review pages and their order, which stands; what is set aside is its hold on the run. Plants takes the same change in the same increment.

conflicts.about: Where a journey page's Back link goes

positions.says: Back goes to the template review when reached from one, to the overview when reached from the hub, and otherwise to the previous journey page.

conflicts.about: Whether the origin of the import page offers 'Save and return to overview' and 'Cancel and return to overview'

conflicts.about: Whether the party pickers, the CPH number page and the permanent address page offer return-to-hub controls

positions.says: A DR1 judgement on the same difference overrides the prototype default.

Under rule (b) the party pickers end with the primary button alone.

conflicts.about: Whether the journey keeps a contact address page whose return controls say 'hub'

conflicts.about: Which controls the party pickers, the CPH number page and the permanent address page show while a notification is being amended

The animals suite now proves the behaviour on the main import reason, arrival details, commodity details, transporter list and commodity selection pages (repo-tests-p4-125 to repo-tests-p4-131). conflicts.about: Whether the service navigation keeps a Log out item: the target design drops it, and the deployed services have it.

positions.says: In DR2.1 the service navigation has no Log out item, unlike design release 2.

conflicts.about: Which today source says what the animals frontend does now, where the fit and end-to-end traces disagree with the frontend's own source and the test suite.

The hint is the clearest instance, and the same holds for the inset, the search running as the trader types, the live-region announcement, the bold matched text, the species chips and their Remove names, the Save and continue that now reaches the import reason page, the back link that follows the journey, the Selected commodities table's headings and the catalogue's Cattle naming. Two claims of the 9 October templates ruling are not set aside, because each still backs something true: ruling-sam-2026-10-09-templates-p1-032 records that template mode walked the same pages rather than changing them, which is why parking templates leaves the commodity pages as they are, and ruling-sam-2026-10-09-templates-p1-052 records that template mode was animals only, which the templates area keeps as the record of what is parked. conflicts.question: Do the destination country and port of exit questions keep the accessible autocomplete the animals frontend now has, or go back to plain selects as the 9 October afternoon ruling's plain-select clause says?

Paul's point that no type is stored stands in full (ruling-paul-2026-11-05-p1-022). Nothing is overruled: both behaviours are what the service already does, and req-1256 states them.

conflicts.about: Whether the add-details step holds its roles error back until the address and contact fields are valid, or shows it with them.

positions.says: The usage question is checked only once the address and contact fields are valid.
Saving with every field empty and no use ticked shows only the six text-field errors.
On a save the trader sees an error message for each answer that is missing or not valid.
A real constraint the prototype cannot express, such as validation, overrides the prototype.
The roles error is listed after the address and contact field errors in the summary.
When a field is invalid and no role is ticked, the error summary lists both messages in page order.

conflicts.outcome: The 26 October ruling's per-answer rule and the 7 October ruling's validation clause both outrank the prototype, and they agree: one save reports every missing or invalid answer, the roles among them, so an error summary never hides a second round of errors behind the first. The service already behaves this way (repo-insfrontend-p5-079, repo-tests-p13-033), and the edit page's roles error follows the same rule (req-2795). prototype-dr2-1-source-p16-076 is not overruled, because its message and its link target are what req-1255 builds; only the order it checks in is set aside, and trace-prototype-dr2-1-p18-079 shows that order rather than anything else to build.

conflicts.about: Whether the edit page's Country select drops its blank option, given an address whose stored country code the list no longer offers and a save that must still be refused with 'Select a country'.

positions.says: The edit form's country select has no blank placeholder and shows the stored country selected.
A real constraint the prototype cannot express, such as validation or persistence, overrides the prototype.
On an edit form the country select leaves out the placeholder when the saved country is in the list, and shows it when it is not.
An address whose stored country code is not one the select offers opens the edit page on the select's blank option.
Saving the edit page without choosing a country is refused with 'Select a country' and the stored code is left as it was.

conflicts.outcome: The prototype's edit form cannot express either case: its country list is fixed, so no stored code is ever missing from it, and it never refuses a save for one. The 7 October ruling's validation and persistence clause settles both. The select offers no blank option while the stored country is one the list offers, which is Design Release 2.1's look; where the stored code is not offered the select opens blank rather than silently showing another country, and that blank state is what 'Select a country' refuses on save (req-1234). The service already does this (repo-insfrontend-p5-102). Nothing is overruled: the prototype still decides the select's look for every address whose country MDM still serves.

conflicts.about: Whether the address book's add-details step asks for a county.

positions.says: The address book's add-details step keeps its County field; it is not removed.
This decision replaces inc-062's criterion that the add-details step has no County field.
County is a field of the Standard Address Block, marked Optional.
The Design Release 2.1 add-details step has no County field, unlike the root address book manual fields.
The edit page has an optional County field, which the add pages do not have.
The add-details form carries a County field, marked optional, between Town or city and Postcode or Zip code.

conflicts.outcome: Paul's ruling of 14 October ranks above the prototype and keeps County on the add-details step, labelled 'County (optional)' between 'Town or city' and the postcode (req-2363). Its grounds are the V4 Address Block, which gives every address block the same fields with County among them and outranks the prototype, and the round trip: an add form that cannot set a field the record, the view page and the edit form all carry would lose it. Design Release 2.1 leaving the field out is therefore a prototype mistake, and prototype-dr2-1-source-p16-045 is set aside; req-1225, which asked for the field to go, is out of scope and keeps the claim as the record of what was set aside. trace-prototype-dr2-1-p18-116 is not overruled: it also shows the edit page's County field, which req-1226 keeps. The field keeps the 100-character cap the record and the add and edit forms already enforce.

conflicts.about: Which environments' saved addresses are deleted when the address book starts storing roles, beyond dev, test and a local stack.

positions.says: The entire addresses collection is deleted on the two shared environments, dev and test, using CDP tooling, because none of the addresses already saved has any value.
Locally the stack is restarted instead of dropping a collection with CDP tooling.
The ruling says nothing about what happens to addresses saved before the change in any environment beyond dev, test and a local stack.
A stored address's roles may be null or empty: the record itself does not require a role, only the request does.
Roles are optional on the stored document, so a record can be held with none.

conflicts.outcome: Nothing ranks the readings: the ruling names dev, test and a local stack and is silent on every other environment, and a record saved before the change can still be held with no role at all, so an address without a role would reach a picker that filters by role. Each part of the target therefore gets what the default below says until the owner answers, and req-2359 waits on it.
conflicts.question: Besides dev, test and a local stack, which environments have their addresses collection dropped when the address book starts storing roles, and what happens to an address already saved there?
conflicts.default: After the change is released, dev and test have the whole addresses collection dropped with CDP tooling and the address book restarted, and a local stack is restarted. perf-test and ext-test are dropped the same way when the change reaches them, because their addresses are test data too. Pre-production and production are not touched and no address is deleted there, the service not being live for traders yet; if an address without a role is ever found in either, it is left in place and no picker offers it, rather than being deleted or given a role.

conflicts.about: How an add reached from a notification journey treats the roles question: shown with the hand-off's role ticked, hidden with that role applied, or offering only the party's other roles.

positions.says: In the role-handshake mode the roles question reads 'What else should this address be used for?' and offers only the other roles on the party's side, unticked.
In the role-handshake mode no role need be ticked, and the address is saved with the party's own role plus any other roles ticked.
Save and select on a hand-off gives the address the party's role without the user ticking any role, so a journey-reached add form does not ask the roles question the address-book-reached one does.
A journey section starting an address book add records where to return and suggests that section's address type.

conflicts.outcome: The INS front door's own extract, which ranks above the end-to-end suite, now shows what the journey-reached add does, and it answers the earlier question: the page asks 'What else should this address be used for?', names the party in its hint, offers only the other roles on the party's side unticked, leaves the question out when there are none, and saves the party's own role plus any ticked (req-2360). The suite's reading that the journey form asks no roles question is set aside as a reading of the code; its proof that the party's role is saved without a tick stands, so the claim is not overruled. The prototype's journeys add addresses on their own pages and say nothing of this page, so they do not rank against it.

conflicts.about: What the addresses section, card and task row on the templates pages are called: the prototype's two names, or the one wording the owner gave on 17 November.

positions.says: The addresses section heading reads 'Addresses'.
The overview page's task row and the check your answers card title read 'Consignment addresses', the same as the addresses page's own heading.
Section numbers stay, so the addresses section heading keeps its number.
The template page's fourth section is headed 'Consignment addresses'.
The card inside that section is titled 'Addresses'.
The template task list's addresses task is headed 'Roles and addresses'.

conflicts.outcome: The owner's decision of 17 November ranks first and gives one wording everywhere the addresses appear: the section heading reads 'Addresses' and keeps its number, while the task row, the card title and the addresses page's own heading all read 'Consignment addresses'. On the templates pages that swaps the prototype's two names over: the template page's and the template review's fourth section is headed 'Addresses' and holds a 'Consignment addresses' card (req-1346, req-1352, req-2052), the template task list's section is '4. Addresses' with a 'Consignment addresses' task row (req-1330, req-1331, req-1353), and a notification started from a template has '5. Addresses' (req-1364). The decision reaches the templates pages because template mode walks the same journey pages and the template page and review reuse the review's cards. No claim is overruled: each prototype claim still backs its section's place and contents, the card's rows and the task row's hint; only the two names are set aside.

conflicts.about: How a task list heading is spelled: the prototype's one-word 'tasklist', or the two-word GOV.UK spelling.

positions.says: The notification task list heading reads 'Notification task list'.
'task list' is spelled as two words, which is the GOV.UK spelling.
The overview's task list is a region named 'Notification task list', with the tasks grouped under numbered sections.

conflicts.outcome: The owner's decision of 19 November ranks first and names 'task list', two words, as the GOV.UK spelling of the heading. Its reason is the spelling itself rather than the one page it was given on, so a notification's task list is headed 'Notification task list' and a template's 'Template task list', and one service does not spell the same heading two ways. The prototype's one-word 'tasklist', which this area's working set no longer carries and the overview and templates areas weigh, is set aside; the tests repo's whole walks already read the two-word heading. No claim is overruled.

conflicts.about: Whether templates are built now: the 9 October ruling's create, read, update and delete work that goes ahead, or the later rulings' parked and de-prioritised templates.

positions.says: Templates in Design Release 2.1 are concept work rather than work for the deadline.
A row judged to be concept work is flagged to the owner rather than built.
Templates has been dropped for now.
There is no templates sort to build, and the sort returns as a question only if templates do.
Templates is de-prioritised, which is why the type question page is split away from it.
The templates rows stay in their theme, parked, and are not built now.
Templates are simple create, read, update and delete work and go ahead now.

conflicts.outcome: The later rulings rank first and reverse the 9 October ruling's 'now': templates are concept work, de-prioritised, dropped for now, and their rows stay parked and are not built. So every adopted templates requirement keeps its wording and carries the owner's decision to pick templates up again as its blocker, and the area is re-distilled when that decision comes; none of them sits in a row to be built meanwhile. Only the 'go ahead now' half of the 9 October templates ruling is set aside, so ruling-sam-2026-10-09-templates-p1-022 is not overruled: it still backs that templates are create, read, update and delete work and what that covers, which is what gets built when the parking lifts. The templates sort stays out of scope whether or not templates return (req-1299), because nothing settles it for a future return. The notification type question page itself is not parked: it is split off into its own theme and goes ahead, and what stays with templates is the template-creation entry to it, whose back link needs Manage templates to exist (req-1314). Neither later ruling names a condition for templates' return, which is why this is a blocker rather than a question.

conflicts.about: Whether 'Amend this notification' on the notification view header stays a posting button in its own form, as the 19 November ruling describes the header built today, or becomes a link to the amend confirmation page once that page exists, as Delete is a link to the delete confirmation page.

positions.says: Once the amend confirmation page exists, 'Amend this notification' is a link to it with no form.
Copy as new keeps a form of its own and Delete stays a link.
The header ruling applies in live animals, germinal products and plants alike.
Each button on the notification view header gets its own form.
The one-form-each rule covers Amend, Copy as new and Delete.
The amend confirmation is a separate page.

conflicts.outcome: The 25 November ruling ranks first and answers this: once the amend confirmation page exists, 'Amend this notification' on the view header is a link to that page, because the first click changes nothing, a POST that only renders a page is the wrong verb and leaves a re-POST on the back button without JavaScript, and Delete already opens its confirmation page by href. Copy as new keeps its own form because it still changes something, Delete stays a link, and no action shares another's form, in live animals, germinal products and plants alike. The 19 November ruling is not weakened, its subject being that no action shares another's form, which a link does not do; its claims are not overruled, because they still back Copy as new's own form and Delete outside it.

conflicts.about: Whether a 'Submitted action required' status exists for the actions on a submitted notification to accept.

positions.says: New statuses are added only, alongside the existing ones.
A submitted notification with outstanding items is 'Submitted action required' with an orange tag.
No 'Submitted action required' status is introduced.
A notification submitted with outstanding items is SUBMITTED like any other.
Nothing action-required is shown until the banner design is agreed.
The suite models four statuses.

conflicts.outcome: The 16 November ruling ranks first and withdraws the status: a notification submitted with outstanding items is SUBMITTED, so amend, copy as new and delete accept it as they accept any submitted notification and nothing extra is built for it (req-2113 goes out of scope). Outstanding actions wait for the banner-style alert the dashboard designs under test introduce. The design's action-required status claim is overruled, because the state it rests on does not exist; the add-only status rule is not overruled, because it still governs the completed status (req-2114).

conflicts.about: Whether a copy maps a certified-for value the set no longer offers onto a current one, on the list of values the prototype's own code holds.

positions.says: An older certification purpose is mapped to a current option when copying.
No row rests on the prototype's demo fixtures for which values a field offers.
Every piece of data is MDM content or V4-specified.
V4 is the source of truth for data.
The prototype still decides how a page looks and reads, not its data.

conflicts.outcome: The 11 November ruling ranks above the prototype on data: the certified-for question's values are the data dictionary's and the reference lists', and the prototype's mapping is a list of its own retired options, so there is no row in it. A copy carries certified-for over as stored (req-1429, req-1431), which keeps the germinal set's own answer without a rule of its own, so req-1430 and req-1879 go out of scope and the prototype's mapping claim is overruled. Nothing bars a later row on retired values if the data dictionary or a reference list ever retires one.

conflicts.about: Whether submitting a notification records the outstanding items left at the moment of submission.

positions.says: The animals backend stops storing the outstanding items list, the health-certificate-owed list that nothing reads, and the rule that works it out comes off the outstanding-item type; both are re-added later with the future outstanding-actions banner.
This call replaces the 16 November ruling's clause that kept the outstanding items, so that ruling no longer keeps them; only the submitted date stays.
Submitting a notification records the outstanding items left at the moment of submission, because a future banner needs them.

conflicts.outcome: The 19 November ruling is the later word and ranks above the 16 November one, and it names the clause it replaces, so the record holds no outstanding items list and nothing derives one from the outstanding-item type; the backend already stores nothing about what is still owed (repo-backend-p1-011-m1). The submitted date is carved out of the supersession and is still recorded (ruling-sam-2026-11-19-p1-024, met by req-1499). The list and its rule come back with the outstanding-actions banner, whose trigger neither ruling names. ruling-sam-2026-11-16-p1-011 is overruled; the same ruling's submitted-date claim p1-010 is not, because it still backs what is kept.

conflicts.about: Whether a 'Submitted action required' status is added beside the four lifecycle statuses.

positions.says: No new 'Submitted action required' status is introduced, and the 9 October afternoon ruling's status is withdrawn.

A notification submitted with outstanding items, such as a missing health certificate, has the status SUBMITTED like any other, because a status that does not align with the notification flow is not introduced.
Outstanding actions are shown through a banner-style alert the dashboard designs under test introduce, and nothing action-required is shown until that design lands.
The add-only status rule covers 'Submitted action required' and, once unblocked, 'Completed'.
A new status is mirrored in plants only where plants has the same lifecycle, and 'Submitted action required' rests on the ITAHC and is animals only.

conflicts.outcome: The 16 November ruling ranks above the 9 October afternoon one: no 'Submitted action required' status is added, so the enum stays at DRAFT, SUBMITTED, AMEND and DELETED (req-1497, req-1987), a notification submitted with outstanding items is SUBMITTED like any other, and outstanding actions wait for the banner design. Neither p2-071 nor p2-076 is overruled, because each still backs something true: p2-071's add-only rule still covers 'Completed' once a real source of completion exists, and p2-076's rule that a status is mirrored in plants only where plants has the same lifecycle stands whatever the status is. The 'Action required' tag the same 16 November ruling withdraws from the live-animals list is the notification-list area's to record.

conflicts.about: How the 'answers differ from submitted' flag is held on the notification and whether it is exposed outside the service.

positions.says: 'Answers differ from submitted' is a non-null yes or no flag, and the animals frontend's local stub takes it from the backend's shape rather than working it out itself.
The ruling names neither the flag's field, nor its value for a notification that has never been submitted, nor whether it is published on the notification event.
Each record has an answersDifferFromSubmitted flag that is always true or false, false on a new notification and read as false on a record stored without it.
The fulfilments view returns answersDifferFromSubmitted, and the GBN-AG body does not publish it.

conflicts.outcome: The ruling ranks first and gives the flag's shape to the backend, and the backend on main now has that shape: a root-level answersDifferFromSubmitted flag that is always true or false, false on a new notification and on a record stored without it, returned on the fulfilments view and not published on any event (req-2865). That fills every point the ruling left open in the way the earlier default proposed, so nothing waits on the owner. No claim is overruled: the ruling's claims and the backend's agree.

conflicts.about: Whether the submission event's data is the GBN-AG document or the flat notification summary the tests repo's canned fixture holds.

positions.says: An event's data is the GBN-AG body built from the notification as it stands when the event is written.
The canned submission event the suite keeps carries a flat summary of the notification, with an eventId and a publishedAt the event model does not carry.

conflicts.outcome: repo:backend ranks above repo:tests, and the backend is the service that writes the event, so the published event's data is the GBN-AG exchanged document and specified consignment (req-1567, req-1585). The canned fixture's flat summary is stale test data that no spec reads, and correcting it is out of scope, recorded as an out-of-scope requirement in this area. repo-tests-p9-116 is overruled so no standing requirement rests on the flat shape.

conflicts.about: Whether a decision recorded in the animals frontend's own design record overrides the design release where the two differ.

positions.says: The prototype decides look and feel, and wherever a real service differs from it in look and feel the real service changes to match.
Nothing other than a judgement on the same difference or a real constraint the prototype cannot express overrides the prototype.
The set's design record states the reason the journey's pages look and behave as they do, including choices taken against the way the design draws them.

conflicts.outcome: The two rulings rank above the animals frontend, so a decision recorded in the frontend's own design record is not one of the named overrides. It stands only where it is itself a real constraint the prototype cannot express, or where the data dictionary, an earlier parity judgement or an owner ruling backs it, and otherwise the page changes and the record is rewritten to the reason for the page as built. Nothing is listed as overruled: each recorded choice against the design's own drawing in this area carries a reason another source still backs, the afternoon ruling's rule that the design system's components come first covering both the identification card's summary-card styling and the documents reference cell's break-anywhere class, so none of them stops being built on this conflict alone, and weighing a page's own copy and layout belongs to that page's area.

conflicts.about: Whether the sweep of every other atypical item reaches the exceptions the animals frontend's own record names with a reason.

positions.says: Every other atypical item the engineering review found is fixed, apart from the four exceptions the ruling names.
The ruling does not list the items that sweep covers, so which fixes it reaches has to be read from the engineering review itself.
The set's own record names departures from house rules as deliberate exceptions, each with the reason for it, the documents reference cell's break-anywhere styling class among them.

conflicts.outcome: Nothing ranks the two readings: the ruling's sweep is defined by a list it does not carry, held in an engineering review that is not one of this programme's sources, while the frontend's own record names several departures from house rules as deliberate exceptions. The narrow reading is adopted until the owner says otherwise, so each recorded exception keeps its reason and stays as it is.
conflicts.question: Does fixing every other atypical item cover only the items the 19 November engineering review listed, or also the exceptions the animals frontend's own record names with a reason, such as the documents reference cell's styling class, the county parish holding page's fixed Back target, origin of the import having no return controls and the two transporter details forms' own ending controls?
conflicts.default: Only the items that engineering review listed. Each exception the set's record names keeps its recorded reason and stays as it is, and the record goes on naming it, because each one rests on a real constraint or an accessibility need rather than on a preference.

conflicts.about: Whether the high-risk plants notification view header gains a Copy as new action, which the plants set's own records park.

positions.says: The plants header gains Copy as new, so the live animals and plants headers offer the same three actions: Amend this notification, Copy as new and Delete.
The one-form-each header rule covers Amend, Copy as new and Delete on the notification view header, and applies in both the live animals frontend and the plants frontend.
Copy as new is left out of the plants view header because plants has parked it.
Reusing a previous consignment is parked with no increment of its own: it maps onto the animals Copy as new action, left out of the first pass.
A trader cannot reuse a previous notification: there is no Copy as new action and no notification-copied banner.
The animals post-submission action set is in scope minus Copy as new.

conflicts.outcome: The 25 November (b) ruling, which answered this question against its old default, wins: the plants notification view header offers Amend this notification, Copy as new and Delete, as the live animals header does, with Copy as new posting its own form under the 19 November one-form-each rule and carrying plants' own answers. It is wiring only, because the plants backend's copy endpoint and the frontend's persistence and engine copy are already on main, so the plants backend joins nothing. The 9 October afternoon claim that left Copy as new out, the plants ledger's park of reusing a previous consignment and the specification's no-reuse constraint are set aside. The plants ledger's post-submission action set (repo-plantsfrontend-p16-073) is not overruled, because the rest of it, the list actions, the read-only view's Delete and Cancel amendment and the confirmation's view-or-amend block, still stands; only its 'minus Copy as new' clause gives way, and the ledger records that through a new superseding entry. Which state headers carry Copy as new (a draft's as well as a submitted one's) follows the live animals header, which the manage notifications area decides.

conflicts.about: Whether the high-risk plants journey spec ruling that was deleted rather than superseded is restored, as the set's own convention requires.

positions.says: A ruling changes only through a new numbered entry that supersedes the earlier one, which stays in the ledger marked superseded, and a ruling lives nowhere else.
The plants journey spec ruling that was deleted rather than superseded stays as it is, and the ruling records no interest in changing it.

conflicts.outcome: The 19 November ruling wins: the deleted plants journey spec ruling is not restored and nothing is added to record its removal. The set's convention is not set aside, because it still governs every entry this programme adds to the ledger, so no claim is overruled.

conflicts.about: Whether the high-risk plants address pickers keep the pagination and the restatement of the chosen address that their own records describe.

positions.says: Pagination is kept everywhere, every picker pages at eight and the restatement of the chosen address comes back, the plants contact picker included.
The plants address pickers lose their pagination and their 'Selected address' inset.
A plants picker shows eight addresses a page with pagination beyond that and an inset naming the address already chosen.

conflicts.outcome: The 25 November ruling wins over the 9 October afternoon claim, which it names as an error: every plants picker pages at eight and keeps the restatement of the chosen address. That is what the plants records already describe, so the plants records stand and the pickers need no ledger entry.

conflicts.about: Which high-risk plants pages are signed off, when the engine reads a maturity level from each page but the set's records do not say which page holds which level.

positions.says: A page's maturity is one of exploring, detailing, agreed or readyForLive, a page that sets none is treated as exploring, and a page at agreed or readyForLive counts as signed off.
The set's docs do not say which pages are at which maturity level, so they do not show which pages of the journey are signed off.

conflicts.outcome: Left open. An increment that changes a plants page has to know whether it is changing agreed behaviour, and the set's own records answer that for no page; the one source says both that the level decides it and that the level is not written down anywhere a reader can find it.
conflicts.question: Which high-risk plants pages are at agreed or readyForLive, so an increment that changes one knows it is changing a signed-off page?
conflicts.default: Each page's level is read from its own page identity module and nowhere else, and a page whose module names no level is treated as below agreed, so no plants change is held as a change to a signed-off page unless that page's own module says agreed or readyForLive.

conflicts.about: Whether a journey page's context is carried as the trail the service now writes in the page's address, or as the ?change=1 flag and no trail that the 9 October ruling kept

positions.says: The amend controls keep their content with no action field; exit=hub and ?change=1 stay.
No ?from=hub marker is added; only the live flow's fallback changes.
The return links are treated as blocked, waiting on the save and continue theme, and build once that work has merged.
A journey page's URL may carry a from= query holding the trail of pages the trader came through.
A journey page's address carries the places the trader came by as a from= query, newest last, with the overview, the dashboard and the Import Notification Service as its starting places.
Every journey page's address carries a trail of the places the trader has saved before it.

conflicts.outcome: Unsettled, and the two readings build different services. The 9 October ruling kept ?change=1 and added no marker, and on its plain reading the trail that the save and continue work has since merged into both frontends comes out and the review context goes back to ?change=1. The other reading is that how a service remembers where a trader came from is its own architecture, which the ruling described rather than decided, and that the 10 November ruling deferred the return links to exactly that merged work; the trail then stays and the return and Back rules are specified against it. Precedence ranks neither, because the later ruling defers to the work that built the trail while the earlier one names the flag, and the 27 November ruling settles only the germinal questions, not this one, so the question goes to the owner. Nothing about where a saved page or a Back link goes turns on the answer: the Back and return requirements state those destinations without naming the mechanism.
conflicts.question: Does the journey keep the trail it now writes into each page's address as the way it remembers where a trader came from, or come off it and go back to the ?change=1 flag with no trail?
conflicts.default: The trail stays, in both frontends. A page's address carries the places already saved, newest last, in the service's own names; the review context is the review page's own place on that trail instead of ?change=1; and no page of the merged save and continue work is reverted. New work specifies the return and Back rules by where the trader came from rather than by the query that records it.

conflicts.about: Where a page opened from a Change link on the review page goes when it is saved

positions.says: On look and feel the prototype wins by default over what the real services do today.
A section page returns to the review page when it continues and was reached from the review.
Save and continue on a page opened by a Change link goes on to the next journey page rather than straight back to the review.
Pressing Save and continue from a page opened by a Change link walks every later journey page in turn and ends on the review.

conflicts.outcome: Design Release 2.1 outranks what the real frontend does today and no DR1 judgement or real constraint covers it: a page opened from the review page returns to the review page when it is saved. Walking the rest of the journey from a Change link, which the save and continue work built, is set aside.

conflicts.about: Which environments every link, redirect and form hand-over between services has to work in, and how that is proved, beyond the INS-to-journey hand-over the owner has since settled.

positions.says: Links between services must work in CDP, in the local Docker stack and in the CI Docker stack, all three.
The ruling names CDP as a whole and no environment within it, such as dev, test or production.
The ruling does not say how working links in all three environments are to be proved, so no check or evidence is named.

For the INS-to-journey hand-over, each service takes the other's address from its own configuration, the end-to-end suite proves it in the local and CI Docker stacks, and no new check is built for CDP.
The INS frontend takes every upstream and journey frontend address from its environment configuration.

conflicts.outcome: The 27 November ruling settles the INS-to-journey hand-over: configuration per service, proof by the end-to-end suite in the two Docker stacks and no new CDP check. It does not reach the other cross-service links, such as the animals frontend's Address book item and the address book hand-off back to a journey. For those the 4 November ruling still names CDP as a whole, the programme deploys to some CDP environments and not others, and two readings build different things, so the question stays with a default that says what each part gets.
conflicts.question: Beyond the INS-to-journey hand-over, which CDP environments must every other link, redirect and form hand-over between services be proved in, and what counts as proof there?
conflicts.default: Every link, redirect and form hand-over resolves from the calling service's own configuration with no hard-coded host or port. The end-to-end suite proves each one in the local Docker stack and the CI Docker stack. The INS-to-journey hand-over gets no new check in CDP, as ruled; every other hand-over is walked once by hand on the deployed services in CDP dev and test. CDP perf, pre-production and production take the same configuration and get no proof in this programme.
